newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: East Asia seeks protection of family farmers.
newsitem.headline: East Asia seeks protection of family farmers.

text.p: A group representing small family farmers in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan on Wednesday warned such farms must be protected under international free trade rules to ensure food self-reliance in fast-growing east Asia.
The Far Eastern Agricultural Cooperative Collaboration Council also said the low level of world grain stocks could herald a man-made food crisis.

The council has asked the World Food Summit, scheduled to meet in Rome in November, to prepare a policy framework and the Geneva-based World Trade Organisation to devise new trade rules to spur domestic food production, particularly of staple foods.
In Asia, billions of small family farmers played a vital role in maintaining food security and rural stability, the council said in a statement.
It said the farms must be supported and protected.
The world's farmers would be asked to feed 7.9 billion people 25 years from now, up 39 percent from today, an agricultural forum sponsored by the council was told on Wednesday.
"In the new agricultural trade rules, production of staple foods for domestic consumption should be exempted from the commitment to trade liberalisation," the council said.

Nine of every 10 new births would occur in developing countries, while grain self-sufficiency fell to 88 percent in 1993-95, from 96 percent in 1969-71, said Gary Gardner, a research associate at the U.S.-based Worldwatch Institute.
"In the face of increased global demand and faltering production, the need to care for agricultural resources is more urgent than ever," he told the forum.
Grain reserves averaged the equivalent of 104 days of global consumption in 1987 but had fallen steadily to 50 days' worth in 1995 -- the lowest level on record, Gardner said.
The council said it was deeply concerned about the recent dramatic increase in grain prices on the world market.
It also warned of further environmental destruction which could eventually undermine global food security if all the rules of free trade were applied to the agricultural sector.
